Menstrual Hygiene: An Awareness Guide
Overview
Menstruation is a normal, healthy biological process experienced by girls and women, typically beginning between ages 10 and 15 and continuing on a monthly basis until menopause. Practicing good menstrual hygiene helps prevent infections, supports comfort and confidence, and allows girls and women to continue their daily activities, including school and work, without disruption. Understanding the facts about menstruation and addressing it openly within families and communities helps reduce stigma and supports better health outcomes for adolescent girls and women.
Key Facts
A normal menstrual cycle usually lasts around 21 to 35 days, with bleeding typically lasting 3 to 7 days, though this can vary from person to person.
Using a clean absorbent material, such as a sanitary napkin, cloth pad, tampon, or menstrual cup, and changing it regularly (generally every 4 to 6 hours or as needed) helps maintain hygiene and reduce the risk of infection.
Washing the genital area with clean water, and soap if available, during menstruation is recommended; harsh or scented products are generally unnecessary and can sometimes cause irritation.
Hands should be washed with soap before and after changing a menstrual product.
Used sanitary products should be disposed of properly, ideally wrapped and placed in a covered bin, and not flushed down toilets, to support hygienic and environmentally responsible waste management.
There is no medical restriction on bathing, exercising, or carrying out most daily activities during menstruation; in fact, staying active can help ease period-related discomfort for many people.
Menstrual health and hygiene is recognized by national and global public health bodies as an important part of adolescent health, gender equity, and overall well-being, not merely a private or hidden matter.
Common Concerns
Many adolescent girls and their families have questions or worries related to menstruation. Some common concerns include:
Irregular periods: It is common for cycles to be somewhat irregular in the first one to two years after menstruation begins, as the body's hormonal patterns are still stabilizing. Persistent or very irregular cycles beyond this period are worth discussing with a healthcare provider.
Pain or cramps: Mild to moderate cramping during periods is common and can often be managed with rest, a warm compress, light activity, and over-the-counter pain relief if recommended by a doctor or pharmacist. Severe pain that interferes with daily life should be evaluated by a healthcare professional.
Heavy or prolonged bleeding: While flow varies between individuals, unusually heavy bleeding (needing to change protection very frequently) or periods lasting much longer than a week may indicate an underlying condition that should be checked by a doctor.
Myths and social restrictions: In many communities, menstruating girls and women face restrictions around cooking, entering religious spaces, or social participation. These practices are cultural rather than medical, and menstruation does not make a person unclean or make it unsafe for them to carry out ordinary activities.
Access to products: Cost or availability of sanitary products can be a genuine barrier for some families. Government-supported and community programs in several states aim to improve access to affordable menstrual products, particularly for school-going adolescent girls.
When to Seek Medical Advice
While most menstrual experiences are normal, it is advisable to consult a doctor or health worker if any of the following occur:
Periods have not started by around age 15–16, or there is a sudden, unexplained stop in periods after they have been regular.
Bleeding is extremely heavy, requires changing protection more than every 1–2 hours, or includes large clots.
Periods last significantly longer than 7 days on a regular basis.
Severe pain that does not improve with rest or usual pain relief, or that interferes with daily activities.
Unusual vaginal discharge, itching, strong odour, or fever alongside menstrual symptoms, which may indicate infection.
Bleeding between periods or after any long gap since the last period, when not expected.
A local Accredited Social Health Activist (ASHA), Auxiliary Nurse Midwife (ANM), Anganwadi worker, school health counsellor, or nearby Primary Health Centre (PHC) can be a good first point of contact for guidance and referral.
Odisha-Specific Context
The Government of Odisha runs the 'Khushi' scheme, launched by the Department of Health and Family Welfare, to promote menstrual hygiene among school-going adolescent girls. Under this initiative, girls studying in Classes 6 to 12 in government and government-aided schools receive sanitary napkins free of cost, while subsidized napkins are made available to rural women through ASHA workers at a nominal price. The scheme aims to improve access to hygienic menstrual products, reduce school absenteeism and dropout linked to menstruation, and build awareness of healthy menstrual practices. Girls and families in Odisha can reach out to their school health programme, local ASHA worker, or nearby Anganwadi centre for more information or support related to this scheme.
Source Basis
This document is based on general guidance from the World Health Organization (WHO), the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW), the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR), the National Health Mission (NHM), and the Odisha Department of Health and Family Welfare. It does not cite specific studies, statistics, or clinical data, and is intended purely for general awareness purposes.
This content is for general awareness only and does not replace professional medical advice.
